title: Health Insurance
description: Premium, deductible, copay, coinsurance, and the network that changes the bill.
wolfLine: The monthly price is not the bill. Read both.

copay.definition: A fixed amount you pay for a visit or a prescription. The plan pays the rest of its allowed price.
copay.example: A $40 copay at the clinic. The visit’s allowed price is $180. You pay $40.

coinsurance.definition: Your share of a covered bill, as a percent, after the deductible is met.
coinsurance.example: The deductible is met. The bill left is $1,000. At 20% coinsurance you pay $200.

out-of-pocket-maximum.definition: The most you pay in a year for covered, in-network care. After that, the plan pays 100% of covered costs.
out-of-pocket-maximum.example: A $5,000 maximum. Once you have paid $5,000 of deductibles, copays, and coinsurance, covered care costs you $0 for the rest of the year.

special-enrollment.definition: A limited window, generally 60 days, to buy or change health coverage after a qualifying event such as losing other coverage, moving, marrying, or having a baby.
special-enrollment.example: You lose a job’s health plan on March 1. You generally have 60 days to enroll, instead of waiting for the yearly window.

lessons.title: Premium and Deductible
lessons.summary: One is the yearly ticket. The other is the first part of a bill.

steps.context: A health [[premium]] keeps the plan on. The [[deductible]] is what you pay on covered care before the plan shares the bill.
steps.prompt: On a health plan, the premium is:
choices: What you pay to keep the plan active
The first part of each hospital bill
A percent of every bill after the deductible
steps.explain: You pay it in quiet months too.

steps.prompt: The premium is $150 a month. What is that for a year?
Your deductible is $1,500 and you have paid $400 of it. How much deductible is left?
A year with no doctor visits refunds the premium.
steps.explain: The premium bought the plan. It is not a deposit.

steps.prompt: The deductible is the part of a covered bill you pay ___.
steps.explain: Then coinsurance or a copay can take a turn.

lessons.title: Copay and Coinsurance
lessons.summary: One is a flat fee. The other is a percent.

steps.context: A [[copay]] is flat. [[Coinsurance]] is a percent after the deductible.
steps.prompt: What is a copay?
choices: A fixed dollar amount for a visit or a prescription
A percent of the hospital bill
steps.explain: The number does not change with the size of that visit.

steps.prompt: The clinic’s allowed price is $180. Your copay is $40. How much do you pay for that visit?
steps.explain: A copay is the fixed $40, not a slice of the $180.

steps.prompt: The deductible is already met. Coinsurance is 20% of $1,000. How much do you pay?
How much does the plan pay of that $1,000?
Coinsurance is a second premium you pay every month.
steps.explain: It shows up on a bill, after the deductible, not on the monthly premium.

lessons.title: One ER Visit
lessons.summary: Deductible first. Then the percent. Then the yearly cap.

steps.title: The bill, in order
steps.body:
This plan’s ER has no copay. The deductible is **$1,500** and none of it is met. Coinsurance is **20%** after that. The out-of-pocket maximum is **$5,000**.

The bill is **$2,500**.

steps.context: An [[out-of-pocket maximum]] caps what you pay in a year for covered, in-network care.
steps.prompt: How much of the $2,500 goes to the deductible?
steps.explain: The whole $1,500 deductible is still open.

steps.prompt: Coinsurance applies to the other $1,000. At 20%, how much is that?
How much do you pay in total for this visit?
The out-of-pocket maximum is $5,000. After this $1,700, how much room is left before the plan pays covered care in full?
Once you hit the out-of-pocket maximum, the plan pays 100% of covered in-network care for the rest of that year.
steps.explain: That is the cap. It does not include the premium, and it does not include care the plan never covered.

lessons.title: A Plan Summary
lessons.summary: Four numbers. Do not mix them up.

steps.context: The summary is the cover. The network note matters as much as the dollars.
steps.prompt: What is the yearly premium?
steps.explain: That line is $2,400.

steps.prompt: What is the office-visit copay?
steps.explain: That line is $40.

steps.prompt: What is the out-of-pocket maximum?
steps.explain: That line is $5,000.

steps.prompt: Which number is the monthly-style price of keeping the plan, shown here for the year?
steps.explain: The premium is the ticket. The copay is a visit. The maximum is the yearly cap.

steps.prompt: These dollar figures apply to every out-of-network doctor automatically.
steps.explain: The page says in-network. Out of network is a different, usually worse, set of numbers.

lessons.title: In Network or Out
lessons.summary: The same doctor can be a bargain or a surprise.

steps.context: In-network care uses the plan’s prices. Out-of-network care often costs you more, and it may not count toward the [[out-of-pocket maximum]].
steps.prompt: What does in-network mean?
choices: The doctor or hospital has a deal with your plan
The doctor is the closest one to your house
steps.explain: The deal is why the allowed price is lower.

steps.prompt: Going out of network usually costs the same as staying in.
steps.explain: The plan’s deal stops at the edge of the network.

steps.prompt: You need a specialist. What do you check before the visit?
choices: That they are in network for this plan
Only that they have a diploma on the wall
That their office is painted blue
steps.explain: A great doctor can still be an out-of-network bill.

steps.prompt: An in-network hospital uses an out-of-network surgeon. What is the risk?
choices: Part of the bill may be priced as out of network
steps.explain: The building and the doctor can be on different lists. Ask.

steps.prompt: Care with a doctor who has a deal with your plan is ___.
steps.explain: That deal is the discount.

lessons.title: HMO or PPO
lessons.summary: One plan wants a home base. The other lets you roam.

steps.context: These are two common shapes. An emergency is treated differently from a planned visit.
steps.prompt: Which setup is this?
items: You pick a primary doctor and get referrals to specialists
You can see a specialist without a referral
The network is usually smaller and the premium often lower
The network is usually larger and the premium often higher
Out-of-network care is rarely covered, except emergencies
steps.explain: An HMO is a tighter list and a home doctor. A PPO costs more and lets you move around.

steps.prompt: You want to see a dermatologist without asking a primary doctor first. Which shape fits?
steps.explain: The PPO is the one that skips the referral.

steps.prompt: An HMO and a PPO always charge the same premium.
steps.explain: The PPO’s extra freedom is usually not free.

steps.prompt: You rarely leave one clinic and you want a lower premium. Which shape is built for that?
choices: A policy with no network at all
steps.explain: A smaller list is the HMO’s bargain.

steps.prompt: An HMO usually asks you to start with a ___ doctor.
steps.explain: That doctor is the front door.

lessons.title: Two Plans
lessons.summary: A quiet year and a sick year pick different winners.

steps.context: Same coinsurance. The premium and the deductible are the contrast.
steps.prompt: What is Plan A’s premium for a year?
What is Plan B’s premium for a year?
How much more premium does Plan A cost per year?
You expect almost no care. Which plan costs less if that comes true?
steps.explain: With no bills you pay the premium. $1,080 is less than $2,880.

steps.prompt: You expect a large bill and you want the smaller deductible. Which plan is that?
why: B is the cheap premium, not the small deductible.
steps.explain: A’s deductible is $500. B’s is $3,000.

steps.prompt: The lower premium is the better plan for every person.
steps.explain: It wins a quiet year. A big bill can make the low deductible worth the extra premium.

lessons.title: Luis on the Marketplace
lessons.summary: The yearly window is posted. A life change can open a shorter one.

story.title: The window and the discount
story.body:
Luis’s café does not offer health insurance. He has been uninsured since he turned 26 and left a parent’s plan. The yearly [[open enrollment|open-enrollment]] window for work benefits is not his door. His door is HealthCare.gov, and he should check that site for this year’s dates.

In this example a plan’s premium is **$180** a month. An income-based discount brings his example premium to **$70**. He also learns that losing coverage, moving, marrying, or having a baby can open a special enrollment period of generally **60** days.

steps.context: [[Special enrollment]] is the extra window, generally 60 days, after a qualifying event. Income-based Marketplace discounts are real, and the dollar amount depends on the year and the household.
steps.prompt: In the example, how much less is the discounted premium per month?
How much is that example discount over 12 months?
A special enrollment period is generally how many days?
steps.explain: About 60 days after the qualifying event. Check HealthCare.gov for the rule that applies to you.

steps.prompt: Luis loses no job coverage, does not move, and does not have a baby. He simply waited. What is true?
choices: He uses the yearly window posted on HealthCare.gov, not a special enrollment period
A text message can sell him a legal exception
steps.explain: Special enrollment needs a qualifying event. The yearly window is the ordinary door.

steps.prompt: An income-based discount is the same dollar amount for every shopper.
steps.explain: It depends on income, household, and the year’s rules.

lessons.title: Sharpen Up
lessons.summary: Smart repetition on what you’re closest to forgetting.

lessons.title: Den Trial: Health Insurance
lessons.summary: 8 questions. Three strikes and you’re out.

steps.prompt: Premium $200 a month. What is the yearly premium?
The deductible is met. You owe 20% of a $500 covered bill. What is that share called?
steps.explain: A percent after the deductible is coinsurance.

steps.prompt: Out-of-network care usually costs the same as in-network care.
steps.explain: The plan’s prices stop at the network.

steps.prompt: Out-of-pocket maximum $4,000. You have paid $2,500. How much room is left?
